Prevention: Avoid heavy/clay soils because they are poorly drained and lead to root rot and cause poor trees.
Sandy or loam soils are good
Orange trees are self-shaping, but pruning minimizes fresh long shoots preferred by aphids
Clear bushes/ weeds in and around orchard to reduce alternative hosts of aphids.
But keep flowering weeds as they provide nectar for natural enemies.
Also keep dry residues as mulch.
Monitoring: Aphid populations on trees are high after rains when it is warm and green plants are few
Aphids are tiny, less than 3 mm long, pear-shaped soft insects.
Some are light-greenish, others yellowish, brownish or black.
They stay in groups which are seen with naked eyes.
Search under leaves and on growing tips
But not each leaf curling is caused by aphids.
Look under leaves to confirm aphids
Aphids produce sticky substance (honey dew) found on leaves, which attract ants
Young trees suffer more from aphids than old trees.
At 4 to 6 small aphid colonies per 1 to 2 m branch consider action.
However, if every second or third colony has natural enemies, no action is needed.
Look for ladybird adults or larvae, hover fly larvae, lacewing larvae, light brown dry round aphid mummies
Direct Control: Pick heavy infested leaves and shoots at early infestation on small trees
Wash aphids off the tree with a hard spray from a hose every 3-4 days
Make a hot pepper solution, 25g-50/L of water, filter and spray at cloudy weather
Ferment 20-50g marigold/tagetes flowers/1L water for 10 days, stir daily; then filter and spray 1L/2L of water, max 3 sprays.
Soak 20-50g/L of water of neem cake/powder for 12-24 hours filter and spray
